==Education==
Bateson was educated at [[Westminster School]] and [[King's College, Cambridge]]<ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | author=Anon|year=2017|title=Bateson, Prof. Sir (Paul) Patrick (Gordon) | id = U6789 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.6789}}</ref> where he was awarded a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[zoology]] in 1960 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] for research on [[ethology|animal behaviour]] supervised by [[Robert Hinde]].<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|title=The Development of Filial and Avoidance behaviour in the domestic chicken|first=Paul Patrick Gordon|last=Bateson|date=1963|url=http://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/23483522?style=html|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.449192}}|website=Copac.jisc.ac.uk|oclc=500380329|access-date=11 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181118205639/https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/23483522?style=html|archive-date=18 November 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=nobit/><ref name="Bateson2015">{{cite journal|last1=Bateson|first1=Patrick|title=Patrick Bateson|journal=Current Biology|volume=25|issue=5|year=2015|pages=R180–R181|issn=0960-9822|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2014.12.040|pmid=25897438|doi-access=free|bibcode=2015CBio...25.R180B }}</ref><ref name="cambridge" />

==Career and research==
Bateson was a biologist who specialised in researching the behaviour of animals and how it is influenced by genetic and environmental factors. He was a world authority on [[Imprinting (ethology)|imprinting]] in birds – the process of learning to recognise their parents and members of their own species – and his work led to new principles in behavioural development.<ref name=frs>{{cite web|title=Professor Patrick Bateson FRS|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815135948/https://royalsociety.org/people/patrick-bateson-11050|archive-date=2017-08-15|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/patrick-bateson-11050|website=Royalsociety.org|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|author=Anon|year=2017}}

One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where:{{blockquote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]].” --{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2017-08-24 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111170346/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies |archive-date=11 November 2016 }}}}</ref>

Bateson devised original experiments that showed how characteristics of imprinting depend on the bird's early life experiences. Bateson's investigation of learning in birds has led to greater understanding of the neural basis of memory. He had an interest in how developmental and behavioural processes influence evolution.<ref name=frs/>

Bateson was concerned with the ethics of using animals in research and the analysis of animal pain and suffering. This led to a study exploring the effects hunting with hounds had on red deer, an inquiry into dog breeding, and a review of the use of animals in research.<ref name=frs/>

Previous academic positions include a [[Harkness Fellowship]] at [[Stanford University]]<ref name=nobit/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/batesonp.html|title=Patrick Bateson profile|website=Edge.org|access-date=22 December 2004|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160908054547/https://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/batesonp.html|archive-date=8 September 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> and ten years as head of the Cambridge sub-department of Animal Behaviour. Bateson served five years as biological secretary to the Royal Society and fifteen years as [[Master (college)|provost]] of [[King's College, Cambridge]], retiring from both in 2003.<ref name=rsbm/> He retired from his Cambridge Chair in 2005.

Bateson published on such topics as ethology, [[animal welfare]], behavioral development and [[evolution]].<ref name=nobit/>

===Awards and honours===
Bateson was [[knight bachelor|knighted]] for services to science in the [[2003 Birthday Honours]] list. He received an Honorary [[Doctor of Science]] (ScD) degree from the [[University of St Andrews]]<ref>[http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/news/archive/2001/title,42364,en.php Honorary degrees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305073809/http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/news/archive/2001/title,42364,en.php |date=5 March 2016 }}, St-andrews.ac.uk; accessed 18 February 2017.</ref> and an honorary fellowship from [[Queen Mary University of London]].<ref>[http://www.qmul.ac.uk/alumni/notablealumni/honoraryfellows/ Honorary Fellows] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160927032529/http://www.qmul.ac.uk/alumni/notablealumni/honoraryfellows/ |date=27 September 2016 }}, qmul.ac.uk; accessed 18 February 2017.</ref>

He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1983.<ref name=frs/> In 2014 he received the [[Frink Medal]] from the [[Zoological Society of London]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.zsl.org/sites/default/files/media/2018-06/Frink%20Award%20Winners.pdf|title=Winners of the ZSL Frink Medal for British Zoologists|publisher=ZSL|access-date=18 September 2019}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Patrick Bateson's grandfather's cousin was the [[geneticist]] [[William Bateson]]. Patrick's daughter is Melissa Bateson, also a professor of ethology, at [[Newcastle University]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Davies |first=Nick |author-link=Nicholas Barry Davies |date=January 2018 |title=Sir Patrick Bateson 1938–2017  |journal=[[Ibis (journal)|Ibis]] |language=en |volume=160 |issue=1 |pages=253–254 |doi=10.1111/ibi.12550|doi-access=free }}</ref> Patrick Bateson was an atheist.<ref>"A confirmed agnostic, he [Bateson] was converted to atheism after attending a dinner where he tried to converse with a woman who was a creationist. "For many years what had been good enough for Darwin was good enough for me. Not long after that dreadful dinner, Richard Dawkins wrote to me to ask whether I would publicly affirm my atheism. I could see no reason why not." " Lewis Smith, 'Science has second thoughts about life', The Times (London), 1 January 2008, Pg. 24.</ref> He died on 1 August 2017 at the age of 79.<ref name=nobit/><ref name=whoswho/><ref name="guardianobit">{{cite news|last1=Martin|first1=Paul|title=Sir Patrick Bateson obituary|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/aug/14/sir-patrick-bateson-obituary|access-date=15 August 2017|newspaper=The Guardian|date=14 August 2017}}</ref>
